messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000062

From text 'manual–chapter2024pressuresystemssafety pages 22-25'.

GS Manual–Chapter. Pressure systems safety w/change 2 (11/15/2024). Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt treats pneumatic testing as a high-hazard alternative because compressed gas stores significant energy that can be released during vessel or piping rupture. Potential consequences include high-velocity shrapnel, explosive noise, cutting action from small leaks, pressure waves, and movement or projectile-like propulsion of failed equipment. The text does not provide a separate stored-energy calculation specifically for small vessels, but it requires secure fastening to prevent hazardous movement and mandates the two-person buddy system. An exclusion or restricted zone must be calculated using Appendix B; it is based on the distance at which blast overpressure reaches 0.5 psi, a level that may shatter windows. The area must be barricaded or patrolled, and additional controls may include blast walls, personnel evacuation, remote placement, signs, and barriers. Pneumatic testing may replace hydrostatic testing only when the system cannot safely be filled with liquid, cannot be dried and cannot tolerate residual test medium, or hydrostatic testing would damage linings, insulation, or equipment. Before authorization, the procedure and supporting documents must be reviewed, and a Pneumatic Test Request and Permit are required. A low-pressure leak test is required beforehand, and combination tests require the same precautions as pneumatic tests.


---

## pqac-00000063

From text 'edwards2011evaluatingandreducing pages 1-2'.

VH Edwards, D Sanford, and B Bonstead. Evaluating and reducing the risks of pneumatic pressure testing. Unknown journal, 2011.

The excerpt identifies compressed-gas stored energy as the principal hazard in pneumatic testing. At test pressures around 100 barg, stored pneumatic energy may be approximately 200 times the stored hydraulic energy, so a rupture can produce blast waves, projectiles, and movement of unrestrained piping or equipment. The text emphasizes that this hazard applies even at lower pressures; an 8-in. pipe segment tested at 18 barg could generate 0.5 psig overpressure at 28 m. Exclusion zones must prevent personnel from entering the area surrounding the vessel or piping under test. The excerpt defines the exclusion zone in the table as the radius within which overpressure exceeds 0.5 psig, with example values for 8.625-in. pipe ranging from approximately 29–51 m, depending on material and pressure; these figures are piping examples rather than universal small-vessel distances. Pneumatic testing is presented as an alternative when hydraulic testing is undesirable, particularly for LNG and cryogenic equipment where residual water can cause operational problems or be difficult to remove. It is acceptable only when enhanced design, fabrication, and nondestructive examination reduce the probability of loss of containment enough for the resulting risk to be acceptable.


---

## pqac-00000064

From text 'arti2018pneumatictestingof pages 4-7'.

Bader Arti, Robert Weyer, Thanh Dang, and Jaan Taagepera. Pneumatic testing of piping: managing the hazards for high energy tests. Volume 3A: Design and Analysis, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1115/pvp2018-84078, doi:10.1115/pvp2018-84078. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt supports a hazard-based approach to pneumatic testing rather than relying only on a fixed stored-energy limit. Pneumatic tests require consideration of both blast-wave effects and fragment throw; exclusion zones should be established accordingly, and additional nondestructive examination or larger exclusion zones may be needed. The cited example involved two 1.4 km DN750 lines tested at 34 bar with 6,675 MJ stored energy and a 200 m exclusion zone under AS 3788—25 times the recommended 270 MJ limit. The test was accepted because several mitigating factors reduced risk: ductile 304L stainless steel, warm conditions, prior hydrostatic testing at 48 bar, 100% RT/UT of site welds, energy distributed over a large area, restricted jetty access, and an Rscaled value above 12. The authors emphasize that stored energy alone can produce inadequate or impractical controls, and that threaded plugs require special attention because fragment-throw exclusion zones can be very large. For test-medium quality, the project used filtered air meeting Class 1 under ISO 8573-1 and performed an ASTM D4285 oil check. The excerpt does not provide specific requirements for small vessels or a dedicated rule stating when vessels unable to tolerate water may be pneumatically tested; it indicates that such acceptance should follow a detailed hazard analysis and applicable standards such as ASME PCC-2.


---

## pqac-00000065

From text '[name redacted]2017asmeboilerand pages 189-190'.

[name redacted], [name redacted], and [name redacted]. Asme boiler and pressure vessel code evaluation and equivalence study for liquefied natural gas facilities. Unknown journal, 2017.

The excerpt describes when pneumatic pressure testing may replace the standard hydrostatic test under ASME BPVC Section VIII, Division 1, Paragraph UG-100. Pneumatic testing is permitted for vessels designed or supported such that they cannot safely be filled with water, and for vessels that cannot readily be dried when service conditions do not tolerate residual testing liquid. Where possible, parts should previously have been hydrostatically tested to the UG-99 pressure. The excerpt compares the 1992 and 2015 requirements: the minimum pneumatic test pressure is generally 1.25 times MAWP multiplied by the lowest stress ratio in 1992, and 1.1 times MAWP multiplied by that ratio in 2015, subject to the applicable limits on calculated test pressure. During testing, metal temperature must be at least 30°F (17°C) above the minimum design metal temperature. Pressure is increased gradually to half the test pressure, then in increments of about one-tenth until the required pressure is reached; it is subsequently reduced for inspection, with leaks corrected and the vessel retested. The excerpt does not specify stored-energy hazard calculations for small vessels, exclusion-zone distances, barricading, or personnel-protection requirements, so those topics require separate safety guidance or governing procedures.


---

## pqac-00000066

From text 'manual–chapter2024pressuresystemssafety pages 15-17'.

GS Manual–Chapter. Pressure systems safety w/change 2 (11/15/2024). Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt establishes hydrostatic testing as the baseline requirement for pressure vessels and systems (PVS). Pneumatic testing, or a combined hydrostatic/pneumatic test, is recognized as an alternate method when the unique circumstances of the system warrant it; the listed alternate method may include an optional low-pressure gas-leak test before the pressure test. However, this excerpt does not specify the particular conditions in which a vessel cannot be filled with water, cannot tolerate residual liquid, or otherwise qualifies for pneumatic testing as an alternative to hydrostatic testing. It also does not provide stored-energy hazard calculations or exclusion-zone distances specifically for small vessels. Any pneumatic test requires a written procedure containing appropriate safety procedures, and that procedure must be approved by both SHeD and the PSM before testing begins. The manual emphasizes that pressure testing is intended to verify structural integrity and protect personnel, and that convenience, schedule, or funding are not adequate reasons to select an alternate method or waive testing requirements. Cryogenic systems additionally require cold-shock testing before pressure testing, but the excerpt does not state that this requirement changes the pneumatic-test approval process.


---

## pqac-00000067

From text 'arti2018pneumatictestingof pages 1-3'.

Bader Arti, Robert Weyer, Thanh Dang, and Jaan Taagepera. Pneumatic testing of piping: managing the hazards for high energy tests. Volume 3A: Design and Analysis, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1115/pvp2018-84078, doi:10.1115/pvp2018-84078. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt provides general hazard and exclusion-zone information relevant to pneumatic testing, although it focuses on piping rather than specifically on small vessels. Pneumatic testing stores substantially more potentially destructive energy than hydrostatic testing because compressed gas is highly compressible. The principal hazards are blast-wave pressure and fragments projected by an explosive rupture. ASME PCC-2 and AS 3788 provide methods or minimum exclusion zones for blast-wave effects, while fragment-throw assessment has historically been less fully defined; the excerpt notes that total stored energy or blast-wave calculations alone may be non-conservative. The 2015 edition of ASME PCC-2 added fragment-throw distances, and the project discussed used a 200 m exclusion zone for tests above 270 MJ. Both cited standards treat piping and pressure vessels together, despite the fact that piping energy is often distributed over a larger area, whereas vessel energy is concentrated in a compact volume. ASME B31.3 normally requires hydrostatic testing but permits pneumatic testing where hydrostatic testing is impractical, such as situations involving residual water concerns or systems unable to tolerate water. The excerpt does not establish vessel-specific stored-energy thresholds, small-vessel criteria, or a complete approval procedure for substituting pneumatic testing.


---

## pqac-00000068

From text '[name redacted]2017asmeboilerand pages 196-199'.

[name redacted], [name redacted], and [name redacted]. Asme boiler and pressure vessel code evaluation and equivalence study for liquefied natural gas facilities. Unknown journal, 2017.

The excerpt provides pneumatic pressure-testing requirements for pressure vessels under the 1992 and 2015 editions of ASME BPVC Section VIII, Division 2. | Topic | Current Design Value | Concern/Finding | Recommendation | Key Source/Standard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 304L/316L dissimilar welding | 304L KF stub to 316L reducer/tube; ER316L GTAW | Metallurgically compatible; dilution, ferrite balance, heat input, and root oxidation matter more than the small grade mismatch. | Retain ER316L; qualify the weld procedure, use low heat input and full argon back-purge, and perform visual plus liquid-penetrant examination. | Related dissimilar-austenitic GTAW studies (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006) |
| Thin wall and KF distortion | 1.65 mm wall; weld about 19 mm from KF flange | Burn-through, angular distortion, and seal-face warping are credible; no source establishes 19 mm as inherently safe. | Fixture and heat-sink the flange, use pulsed GTAW and balanced short segments, then inspect flange flatness, concentricity, and seal-face condition. | Heat-input and HAZ evidence (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005) |
| Sensitisation | 304L/316L base metals and ER316L filler | Low carbon greatly reduces chromium-carbide sensitisation but does not eliminate it after excessive heat input or repeated thermal cycles. | Control heat input/interpass temperature, maintain purge until the root cools, remove heat tint, and passivate. | Sensitisation evidence (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004) |
| Loose liner galling | Loose 304 liner on loose 304 puck | Austenitic stainless contacts can gall; vacuum/inert conditions weaken oxide-film protection. Reported self-mated threshold is about 18 ksi or 124 MPa, but sliding distance and temperature strongly affect damage. | Provide generous clearance, rounded edges, and removal tabs; consider dissimilar sacrificial grades. Avoid hydrocarbon anti-seize in powder service. | Galling and oxidation studies (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035) |
| Thermal stress and shakedown | 86 MPa elastic peak at floor corner; estimated yield 106 MPa at 320 °C; pressure stress 6–7 MPa | Ratios are about 0.81 yield thermal and 0.06–0.07 yield primary. The ideal Bree boundary permits a thermal range near 2 yield when primary stress is below 0.5 yield, suggesting low ratcheting risk; this does not qualify a welded corner or fatigue life. | Model the actual weld radius and residual-stress sensitivity; conduct mesh convergence and several elastic-plastic hot/cold cycles; separately assess fatigue. | ASME VIII-2 Part 5.5.6/5.5.7 and Bree analysis (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000045) |
| Floor geometry | 8 mm flat disc with abrupt internal corner | A sharp modeled corner can create a singular or highly mesh-sensitive peak and is unfavorable for thermal fatigue. | Prefer a shallow dished/radiused floor with a full-penetration butt weld; second choice is a machined generous inside radius or qualified smooth weld contour, not a cosmetic fillet. | Cyclic stress and ratcheting principles (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| FKM seal limit | FKM O-ring; predicted peaks 26/32/45 °C | Generic FKM ratings are about 200–204 °C continuous and roughly 230 °C short-term. Predicted temperatures have ample margin if the thermal model is validated. | Verify the exact compound/vendor rating; retain shielding and replace the seal after abnormal heating or visible hardening/damage. | FKM temperature data (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) |
| Alarm set points | 120 °C top and 150 °C bottom; external washer thermocouples | Conservative relative to FKM limits, but external washer sensors may lag and under-read the inner wall. | Retain the alarms; add rate-of-rise logic and a latched high-high trip validated by representative hot-shot tests. Trip melt input while maintaining inerting and cooling. | FKM limits and high-temperature vacuum practice (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) |
| Melt-arrival detection | Two type-K washer thermocouples | Thermocouples are rugged but indirect; cameras and pyrometers need a protected sight line, while load cells detect abnormal mass but not temperature. | Use TCs as primary sensors; add a hanger load cell if practical. Use a protected two-colour pyrometer or camera for diagnostics rather than as the sole trip. | High-temperature systems use pyrometers and thermocouples (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050) |
| Rate-of-rise leak test | Chamber about 10–20 L at about 10 mbar absolute | Total gas load is Q = V × dp/dt and includes leakage, outgassing, permeation, and temperature effects. No universal acceptance value applies. | Project-specific estimate: Q ≤ 10^-2 mbar·L/s for a gross operational check and preferably ≤ 10^-3 mbar·L/s for repeatable purging. For 15 L these correspond to about 0.040 and 0.0040 mbar/min. Trend against an established baseline. | Pressure-rise method (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000058) |
| Soap/bubble test | Proposed bench soap test | Useful for locating gross positive-pressure leaks but not for demonstrating low vacuum leakage; residues can contaminate the vessel. | Use dry nitrogen or argon at low pressure with commercial leak solution externally, then rinse/dry. Follow with rate-of-rise or helium mass-spectrometer testing. | ASME Section V Article 10 methods and leak-detection guidance (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000057) |
| Hydrostatic proof | Relief set at +0.8 bar(g); proposed proof +1.2 bar(g) | Relief setting is not automatically MAWP. Modern ASME VIII-1 hydrotest pressure is generally at least 1.3 × MAWP times the allowable-stress ratio; older rules used 1.5. Hydrotest stores much less energy than a gas test. | Define MAWP for the complete assembly first. Prefer hydrotesting the welded vessel with a code-rated closure, followed by thorough drying and passivation. | ASME VIII-1 UG-99 comparisons (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000066) |
| Pneumatic proof | Proposed 1.5 × relief setting using KF joint | Modern VIII-1 pneumatic testing is generally about 1.1 × MAWP times stress ratio; VIII-2 uses 1.15. A 1.5 × pneumatic test is not a generic current-code requirement and compressed gas adds rupture energy. | Use pneumatic proof only when hydrotesting/drying is impracticable; apply remote staged pressurisation, restraint, barriers, calibrated relief, and an exclusion zone. | ASME pneumatic ratios and safety guidance (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000068) |

The complete assembly rating is limited by the weakest matched component. | Obtain written manufacturer confirmation for KF-50 size, clamp, centring ring, O-ring, temperature, cycles, and proof pressure. Positively retain the hanging collector and prevent personnel exposure below it. | ISO-KF vacuum-service description (pqac-00000038) |
| Incident lessons | Prior EPDM seat burned and borosilicate cracked; shields now above joint | Published high-temperature vacuum experience shows radiant heat threatening O-rings, cryopumps, and hardware; effective mitigations included water-cooled shielding, close cooling, interlocks, and redundant temperature measurement. Specific peer-reviewed KF positive-pressure incident reports were not found. | Treat the prior event as a credible design-basis upset: preserve a ledge-free bore, shields above the seal, thermal trips, cooling/pressure interlocks, independent support, and post-upset inspection. | TISOL high-temperature operating lessons (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) |

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):

Supported Enums:

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. A university lab is replacing the powder collection container of an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer after a run (0.82 kg of nickel-aluminium bronze, UNS C63000, poured at about 1300 C) produced 1-3 mm
shot instead of powder; the shot piled up on a splash plate and a butterfly valve just under the container's
top seal, burned the EPDM valve seat and cracked the borosilicate tube. The chamber is evacuated to about
10 mbar absolute, backfilled with argon several times and runs at +150 mbar gauge; its relief valve opens at
+0.8 bar gauge. The container hangs from the water-cooled cone's ISO-KF-50 outlet on a hinged clamp.

Final design (please critique, with sources): a TIG-welded vessel, 250 mm long, made of a KF-50 x 2 in
butt-weld stub (304L), a 3 x 2 in concentric butt-weld reducer (316L, 101.6 mm long, 0.065 in wall), a 3 in OD x
0.065 in 316 tube and an 8 mm 316L floor disc (three square-butt / chamfered welds, ER316L, argon back-purge).
Inside: a loose 304 catch puck (70 x 25 mm) on the floor and a loose 304 liner tube (2-3/4 in x 0.065 in) standing
on it, both sacrificial. No valve, no splash plate and no ledge inside the top; the bore only widens below the
seal. A stainless centring ring with an FKM O-ring and an over-pressure ring (rated 50 psig) at the cone joint.
The manufacturer's splash shields (thin discs) lie in the cone's mouth above the joint. Two type K washer
thermocouples under worm clamps: on the stub just below the flange, and 6 mm above the floor, read by a
2-channel meter with relay alarms at 120 C (top) and 150 C (bottom).

Our CalculiX axisymmetric transient model (packed bed of shot at 1050 C, 70 % liquid, k_eff 5 W/m K, pile on the
puck, radiation from the pile top by Monte-Carlo view factors, outside convection 8 W/m2K plus radiation) gives a
peak O-ring temperature of 26 / 32 / 45 C for 100 / 400 / 816 g of shot and a floor peak of about 120 / 255 / 340 C;
a catalogue alternative (KF-50 nipple 160 mm with a blank on the bottom and the puck inside the bottom
centring ring) reaches 128 / 207 / 245 C at its bottom O-ring for 100 / 250 / 400 g. Static FEA gives 7 MPa at
+1.2 bar, 6 MPa under full vacuum and 86 MPa thermal stress at the floor's inside corner (yield about 106 MPa at
320 C).

Questions:
1. What would you change in this design or its materials for this duty (hot copper-alloy shot, Al and Cu alloy
   powders, vacuum/argon cycling)? Any concern with 304L welded to 316L, with ER316L on 0.065 in wall, or with
   sensitisation, distortion of the KF flange 19 mm from a weld, or galling of the loose liner?
2. Is a peak thermal stress near yield at a sharp inside corner of a welded flat floor acceptable for a few
   hundred thermal cycles (shakedown, ASME VIII-2 / III ratcheting rules)? Should the corner get an inside
   fillet weld or a dished floor?
3. Are the alarm set points sensible? What do atomizer or vacuum-furnace operators use to detect unatomized
   melt reaching a collector (thermocouples, pyrometers, load cells, cameras)?
4. Leak and pressure testing: acceptance criteria for a rate-of-rise test on a ~10-20 L chamber at 10 mbar,
   bench soap testing, and whether a pneumatic proof test at 1.5 x the relief setting is appropriate for a
   small stainless vessel with a KF joint (or whether a hydrostatic test is better practice).
5. Any published incidents or lessons on KF joints under positive pressure, over-pressure rings, or elastomer
   seals near hot powder.
Give numbers with sources (standards, vendor technical notes, papers with DOIs) and mark estimates.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study analyzed the mechanical performance of AISI 304 stainless steel joints produced by Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW), a process widely applied in food-processing industries where weld integrity is critical. An unbalanced full factorial design was implemented, considering plate thicknesses of 3 and 6 mm, butt and beveled geometries, and filler materials ER308, ER309, and ER316L. Mechanical testing showed that the highest ultimate tensile strength was obtained with ER309 in butt joints (794.2 MPa), which was 12.4 % lower than that of the base material. Meanwhile, ER316L provided higher ductility, with elongation values close to the base material, and hardness reached 162.5 HB in beveled joints welded with ER309 filler. Impact energy averaged 65 J, with a maximum of 72 J in beveled joints using ER309 filler. Statistical evaluation confirmed that filler alloy was the most significant factor influencing mechanical properties. ANOVA revealed strong effects on tensile strength (F = 6.87, p = 0.03), yield strength (F = 8.45, p = 0.02), elongation (F = 9.12, p = 0.02), and hardness (F = 5.34, p = 0.04), whereas joint configuration and thickness were not statistically significant. Therefore, ER316L is recommended for applications requiring ductility, while ER309 offers advantages in hardness and impact energy, providing practical guidance for industrial implementation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Dissimilar metal welding is a popular process in very large coal and gold, power generation, and pulp and paper factories. It has mainly been applied to produce large boilers in sugar factories. The aim of the present study was to examine the characteristics of dissimilar metal welded joints made from carbon steel and 3CR12 ferritic stainless steel. The welding specimen was made from filler wires of ER308L and ER309L, and a gas tungsten arc welding process was employed for the V-shaped butt weld joints. The effects of the process parameters, such as the microstructural characteristics and mechanical properties, were investigated. The results from the welding parameters with filler wire of ER308L applied at 70A of welding current showed the microstructure of delta ferrite and austenite. In comparison, 100A of welding current presents delta ferrite, austenite, and martensite. Furthermore, carbide formation was not observed in the fusion zones of any of the experiments. When the ER308L filler wire was used, the amount of delta ferrite was higher than that of the ER309L filler wire, and the amount of delta ferrite increased with increasing hardness. In addition, the results of the filler wire of ER308L could replace the ER309L filler wire, which effectively reduces the material cost.

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Rubber O‐rings are vital sealing components in petrochemical and refinery applications, where reliable performance under harsh conditions is essential. This study employs a multianalytical approach to investigate the material composition, curing system, and performance of an industrial O‐ring. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy identified characteristic bands at 1394 cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , confirming the O‐ring as a fluorocarbon elastomer (FKM), with a peak at 3428 cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    (attributed to N–H groups) diminishing post‐Soxhlet extraction, indicating an amine‐based curing system. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) revealed a 91.69% weight loss up to 700°C, with significant degradation at 493°C (58.37% loss between 400 and 550°C) and a residual mass of 8.31%, suggesting minimal filler content. Mechanical testing demonstrated a modulus of 4.60 MPa, tensile strength of 5.86 MPa, strain at break of 165%, and a compression set of 41%, reflecting robust material properties. The O‐ring was identified as Viton A (a vinylidene fluoride [VDF]/hexafluoropropylene [HFP] copolymer) with a diamine curing system, typical of early FKM grades used in demanding chemical environments. While FTIR identifies key functional groups, its integration with TGA (for thermal stability and filler content), Soxhlet extraction (for additive isolation), and mechanical testing provides a practical, accessible framework for reverse engineering industrial elastomers—offering actionable insights into material suitability for petrochemical sealing applications.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rubber O-rings play a crucial role in ensuring the safety and reliability of high-pressure hydrogen systems. However, their degradation and failure under hydrogen exposure remain a major barrier to the long-term stability of sealing structures. This review summarizes the failure modes of rubber O-rings in high-pressure hydrogen environments and clarifies the interaction mechanisms among hydrogen permeation, swelling, rapid gas decompression (RGD), and mechanical fatigue. Compared with conventional high-pressure gases, hydrogen significantly accelerates the coupling of mechanical and physicochemical degradation, leading to multi-mechanism failure characterized by blistering, crack propagation, and modulus reduction. This review highlights the limitations of existing research, including insufficient long-term experimental data, simplified single-mechanism models, and the lack of multi-physics coupling analysis. Future research priorities are proposed in four aspects: (1) development of hydrogen blister-resistant elastomers, (2) collaborative optimization of sealing structures and materials, (3) in-depth investigation of tribological behavior under hydrogen cycling, and (4) establishment of predictive life models integrating multi-scale simulations and experimental validation. This work provides a state of the art of hydrogen-induced failure mechanisms and offers theoretical and engineering guidance for designing reliable sealing systems in next-generation hydrogen energy applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigates the pressure-dependent mechanical behavior and surface degradation of fluorocarbon elastomer (FKM, Viton®) O-ring seals following prolonged high-pressure hydrogen exposure. Specimens were aged at up to 7000 psi for 192 h and evaluated using tensile testing and optical image analysis. The results show a non-monotonic evolution of peak force, stiffness, and energy absorption, with increased load-bearing response at higher pressures accompanied by reduced displacement capacity. Normalized force–displacement behavior shows broadly similar loading profiles across pressure conditions; however, this representation is used for comparative visualization and does not establish preservation of the deformation mechanism. Image-based analysis reveals a significant increase in micro-defect density and surface heterogeneity with pressure, suggesting increased formation of surface micro-defects. These findings highlight pressure-dependent changes in polymer network response and surface morphology under hydrogen exposure. The study provides insights into structure–property relationships governing elastomer performance in hydrogen environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The article presents the results of the development works and research on the atomization process carried out using two prototype high-power ultrasonic systems. Ultrasonic systems have been designed to develop a new metal powder production process; these materials are increasingly used in modern manufacturing processes such as additive technologies or spraying and surfacing processes. The preliminary studies presented in the article were conducted for water to assess the effectiveness of both systems and to verify the theoretical and structural assumptions. In ultrasonic atomization, the ultrasonic wave causes the phenomenon of cavitation, which leads to the overcoming of the surface tension forces of the liquid and its disintegration into fine droplets. The important parameters that affect the properties of the produced droplets include, among others, the frequency of the sonotrode vibrations and the amplitude of the vibrations of the working plate. As part of the research, the paper presents the process of selecting the sonotrode geometry for two different values of the transducer’s natural frequencies (20 kHz and 70 kHz). In the design process, the finite element method was used to perform a harmonic analysis and develop the geometry of the sonotrode and the working plate. The design assumptions and the design process were presented. The modeled and then ultrasonic waveguides were verified experimentally by measuring the deflection distribution on the working plate surface using a high-precision laser displacement sensor. Then, the work ultimately resulted in conducting atomization tests of water. The obtained aerosols and the mechanism of their formation were studied using a high-speed camera. Finally, using Matlab R2020a software and image analysis scripts, it was possible to analyze the droplet size distribution generated by both systems. It was observed that 50% of the produced droplets were in the range of 35–55 μm for a 20 kHz system, while for a 70 kHz system it was 10–25 μm, which is a very satisfying distribution in terms of metal powder atomization.

Abstract:
This paper presents the results of a study on the atomisation process of 316L material. The primary objective of the study was to obtain the highest quality, quantity and yield of 316L metal powder for the established atomisation parameters (torch current and wire feed speed) at the assumed process time. Using experiment planning according to the Taguchi method, 16 pairs of controllable variable parameters were developed. It was observed that the low current high-wire speed configuration resulted in the formation of a considerable amount of molten metal on the sonotrode platform. This phenomenon prevented the ultrasound system from working properly, so some of the processes were interrupted. The results obtained from the tests showed that torch current and wire feed speed are parameters that have a significant impact on the efficiency of the ultrasonic atomisation process. The highest efficiency was achieved by the process with a torch current of 100 A and a wire feed speed of 9 mm/s.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has been intensively studied over this decade due to the increasing demand of functional and precise materials in various industries. AM process leverages on the concept of layer by layer deposition or joining of a material at micro‐ or nano‐scale to produce the final products. As such, AM technology is widely used to manufacture products of complex geometries with high precision in a short time. As the quality and the performance of AM manufactured functional products depend on the quality and the cost of the atomized metal or alloy powder used, the use of powders of high size uniformity, high purity, high sphericity, high flowability, low cost, and no trapped gas bubble porosity is necessary. To this end, various metal production technologies were investigated and one of the popular technologies is atomization. This article reviewed the working principles of the various atomization technologies for the production of fine metal and alloy powders. The technique involves an ultrasonically agitated cold crucible installed at the top of a 20 kHz ultrasonic sonotrode. The material is melted with an electric arc and undergoes pulverization with standing wave vibrations. Several different alloys in various forms, including noble and metallic glass alloys, were chosen to test the process. The AMZ4 metallic glass powder remained amorphous below the 50 μm fraction, while tungsten addition led to crystallization in each fraction. The innovative ultrasonic atomization method appears as a promising tool for material scientists to develop powders with tailored chemical composition, size and structure.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

A novel low-cost gas atomisation technology producing spherical titanium powder (wire induction heating gas atomisation, WIGA) has been developed for additive manufacturing. Combined with the gas atomisation principle, the characteristics of WIGA were analysed. The effects of the gas pressure, metal temperature and the wire-feeding speed on the particle size of the titanium powder were studied. The results indicated that the decreases in mass median particle diameter (D50) and the increases in efficiency of fine size powders occurred with the increase in gas atomisation pressure and melting temperature and with the decrease of wire-feed speed. The optimum parameters are that the main gas pressure (P0) is 4.0 MPa, the degree of superheat of the metal melt is 350°C and the wire-feed speed is 50 mm s−1. On the condition, the D50 of titanium powder was 40.2 μm and powder morphology was spherical. Satellites rarely existed on the surface of particles.

Abstract:
The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) vacuum vessel (VV) is one of the critical components of the ITER tokamak fusion reactor. The first sector of the ITER VV was delivered to ITER Organization in 2020, and it is ready to assemble into the tokamak system. After manufacturing the ITER VV, an evaluation should ensure that the components are designed and manufactured to meet the functional requirements, such as vacuum leak tightness and structural integrity. The factory acceptance test (FAT) is essential for confirming acceptance in engineering and manufacturing. This paper introduces the engineering process and technical method of the FAT, which is applied explicitly to the first-of-a-kind ITER VV. We establish a visual inspection, pre-pumping assessment, pressure test, helium (vacuum) leak test, and final dimensional inspection for the FAT. The visual inspection revealed no blockages in the cooling channels of the double walls. The pre-pumping assessment conducted to check the vacuum level and residual gas condition, concluded that the inside of the VV was flawless and thus met the leak test requirements of 1 × 10−8 Pa m3 s−1. We confirmed no leakage or deformation through the pressure test under reduced pressure. The helium leak test demonstrated engineering soundness with leak tightness of 6.08 × 10−9 Pa m3 s−1, which is more stringent than the allowable limit. Furthermore, three-dimensional metrology was utilized to determine the as-built dimensions of the manufactured sector. Due to unavoidable weld deformation and tight tolerances, the as-built result does not perfectly meet the assigned tolerance level. Nevertheless, it can be considered as advanced information for assembly with in-vessel components and other sectors. Based on the conformance and suitability of the suggested FAT for the first ITER VV sector, we will determine the acceptability of the upcoming VV sectors, which will be manufactured and delivered by Korea shortly.

Abstract:
Pneumatic pressure testing is used extensively during construction of LNG plants to avoid the problems that can be caused by water that may be left in a piping system (particularly in valves) if hydrotesting was performed. Due to the much greater compressibility of gas, there is significantly more energy (and thus risk) associated with a pneumatic test than with a hydrostatic test.
 A major gas project safely conducted numerous pneumatic tests with stored energies of up to 6,675 MJ. Observing a commonly used limit of 270 MJ would have resulted in hundreds of additional closure welds.
 This paper discusses practical aspects of performing pneumatic testing, the risk mitigations put in place and present two calculation methods that can be used to check whether exclusion zones for blast wave pressure are adequate for fragment throw.

Abstract:
A simple testing method to evaluate the influence of high pressure hydrogen gas up to 100 MPa on mechanical properties at the temperature between 20 K and up to 800 K had been developed. In this method, instead of using high-pressure gas vessels, high pressure gas was filled into a small hole in the hollow-type test piece from a hydrogen gas cylinder or a compressor for 10 MPa or 100 MPa test. A small inner diameter of the hole enables to evaluate also the reduction of area in the slow strain-rate tensile (SSRT) tests. The temperature of the test piece with the high pressure gas can be changed simply by surrounding coolant or heater between 20 K and 800 K. Lots of test results by this method proved that almost the same results were obtained between this method and the conventional method with high-pressure gas vessels where test piece is installed. The great advantages of this method are not only the less cost for the facilities of high-pressure vessels but also the ability of tests at lower or higher temperatures than those with the vessels. So, this method is proposed to be used world-widely to evaluate the mechanical properties of structural materials for extremely severe environments, such as high-pressure hydrogen applications and also to study the mechanism of the influence of high-pressure hydrogen for design and reliability of those facilities.
 In this paper, the details of testing procedure of this method and results of tensile and fatigue tests in up to 70 MPa hydrogen gas on several kinds of stainless steels obtained by this method are presented.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'patil2024experimentalinvestigationon pages 2-4'.

Tejas Patil, Ajit Bhosale, S.G.K. Manikandan, Bibin Jose, Mithul Naidu, Sachin Salunkhe, Robert Cep, and Emad Abouel Nasr. Experimental investigation on solidification cracking & intergranular corrosion of aisi 321 & aisi 316 l dissimilar weld on pulsed current gas tungsten arc welding (pcgtaw). Heliyon, 10(15):e34648, Aug 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e34648, doi:10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e34648. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt indicates that concerns in dissimilar austenitic stainless-steel welding include weld-interface thermal stresses, intermetallic or secondary-phase formation, elemental migration, segregation, dilution, reduced corrosion resistance, and solidification or heat-affected-zone cracking. Filler-wire selection and welding procedure are therefore important. Although the source discusses AISI 316L joined to AISI 321 rather than 304L joined to 316L with ER316L, it identifies 316L as generally resistant to high-temperature sensitization and attributes 321’s stabilization to titanium, which limits chromium-carbide precipitation. This supports the view that sensitization is less likely in low-carbon “L” grades such as 304L and 316L than in standard-carbon stainless steels, but it does not establish that sensitization is impossible: excessive heat input, prolonged time in the carbide-precipitation range, repeated passes, or contaminated/poorly controlled welding can still affect corrosion resistance. The excerpt provides no specific guidance for 0.065-inch (1.65-mm) tube. For such thin wall material, the concerns implied by the paper—heat input, distortion, dilution, excessive penetration, HAZ exposure, and cracking—would be especially important, requiring tightly controlled TIG/GTAW parameters and fit-up. No direct ER316L-specific results for the 304L/316L combination are reported.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'patil2024experimentalinvestigationon pages 4-6'.

Tejas Patil, Ajit Bhosale, S.G.K. Manikandan, Bibin Jose, Mithul Naidu, Sachin Salunkhe, Robert Cep, and Emad Abouel Nasr. Experimental investigation on solidification cracking & intergranular corrosion of aisi 321 & aisi 316 l dissimilar weld on pulsed current gas tungsten arc welding (pcgtaw). Heliyon, 10(15):e34648, Aug 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e34648, doi:10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e34648. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt provides related, but not direct, evidence for welding 304L to 316L with ER316L by TIG/GTAW. It identifies elemental migration in dissimilar welds as a concern because it can affect mechanical, metallurgical, and corrosion properties, and it emphasizes careful filler selection with regard to strength, toughness, fatigue and thermal resistance, and hot-cracking tendency. For 304L, the cited study reported that even high heat input did not produce significant carbide or intermetallic precipitation; however, ferrite content and grain size increased while hardness decreased. Thus, the excerpt does not indicate that sensitization is inevitable in low-carbon 304L, but it treats corrosion resistance and possible intergranular attack as issues that should be experimentally checked. The reported procedure used ASTM A262 Practice A, involving oxalic-acid etching and microscopic examination of both HAZ sides. The study itself used 1.6 mm ER316L filler with 5 mm plates under argon PCGTAW, which is dimensionally close to the proposed 0.065-inch (1.65 mm) tube wall, although it does not specifically address thin-wall tubing, distortion, burn-through, purge quality, or heat-control practices. The excerpt therefore supports minimizing excessive heat input and qualifying the weld for microstructure and intergranular corrosion, but gives no direct thin-wall welding recommendations.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'noorbakhsh2026effectoffiller pages 1-2'.

Reza Zare Noorbakhsh, Farhad Ostovan, Ehsan Shafiei, and Meysam Toozandehjani. Effect of filler metals on microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance of gas tungsten arc welded 316ug stainless steel. Materials Today Communications, 57:116584, Dec 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mtcomm.2026.116584, doi:10.1016/j.mtcomm.2026.116584. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides supportive, but not direct, evidence for evaluating TIG/GTAW welding with ER316L between 304L and 316L stainless steels. It describes ER316L as producing fully austenitic weld structures with distributed delta ferrite and the best corrosion performance among the tested fillers in 316UG stainless steel. The study reports tensile strengths above 545 MPa for all joints and fractures in the base metal, suggesting that ER316L weld metal need not be a mechanical weakness under the reported conditions. Regarding sensitization, the article states that low carbon content and stabilizing additions suppress chromium-carbide precipitation and thereby reduce sensitization and intergranular corrosion; it also identifies GTAW’s controlled heat input and narrow HAZ as beneficial. However, the excerpt does not specifically test a 304L-to-316L dissimilar joint, establish allowable heat-input/interpass limits, or address a 0.065-inch (1.65-mm) tube. Consequently, it offers general metallurgical support for ER316L and low-sensitization risk in L-grade steels, but thin-wall welding would still require careful control of current, travel speed, arc energy, fit-up, shielding, distortion, burn-through, and oxidation. The article’s results should not be treated as a qualification for the specific tube geometry or service environment.

URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/engproc2023059090, doi:10.3390/engproc2023059090. This article has 8 citations.

The excerpt provides indirectly relevant information for assessing GTAW of dissimilar stainless steels, although it studies 201/316L rather than 304L/316L and does not specifically address ER316L or thin-wall tubing. It identifies general concerns associated with dissimilar austenitic stainless-steel welding: differences in chemical composition, physical properties, and thermal behavior can promote porosity, solidification cracking, and microsegregation. Ferrite is described as important for reducing solidification cracking, but the amount of ferrite varies with filler-metal chemistry. In the tested 201/316L welds, the 316L filler produced the lowest ferrite number (8.78), compared with 9.05 for 309L and 12.69 for 309LMo. The study also reports sensitization in all filler weldments, ranking highest for 309LMo, followed by 309L and 316L, and associates greater ferrite content and ferrite/austenite interphase regions with higher sensitization. These findings may inform consideration of filler selection, heat input, weld cracking, microstructure, and corrosion behavior. However, the excerpt does not establish whether low-carbon L grades eliminate sensitization risk, nor does it give specific guidance for 0.065-inch (1.65 mm) tube, where welding parameters and heat control would require separate evidence.

It does, however, provide relevant evidence that an E316L weld-metal region can show measurable sensitization: its reported DLEPR degree of sensitization was 9.18%, although this was lower than the E309L and E309LMo weld metals. The authors associate increased sensitization and reduced intergranular-corrosion resistance primarily with greater δ-ferrite content and larger ferrite/austenite interphase regions; the E309LMo result was therefore the most affected. This supports treating sensitization as a possible welding concern even when an L-grade filler is used, rather than assuming low carbon eliminates it under every thermal cycle. The study also reports that the heat-affected zone was softer and that fracture occurred in the 201 stainless-steel HAZ, with the 201-side HAZ wider than the 316L-side HAZ. These observations are specific to dissimilar 316L/201 GTAW and cannot be transferred quantitatively to 304L/316L or thin-wall tubing. Table 4 gives a self-mating threshold galling stress of approximately 18 klbf/in² for both 304–304 and 316–316 contacts. The table also indicates other pairings, including 304 against 316, but the extracted formatting makes some cross-pair values difficult to identify with certainty. The article explains galling mechanistically: under load, asperities deform and oxide or contaminant films may fracture; sliding can then expose fresh, highly active metal and promote strong adhesion. Materials with high ductility, high cross-slip capability, and low work-hardening rates favor plastic asperity deformation, greater energy consumption, rough surfaces, and adhesion. Conversely, low ductility, limited cross-slip, and high work hardening favor asperity fracture and easier sliding. Lower stacking-fault energy inhibits dislocation cross-slip, increases work hardening, reduces total plasticity, and improves galling resistance. This excerpt contains no direct results concerning vacuum or inert atmospheres and no explicit mitigation testing; it supports mitigation concepts involving reduced asperity plasticity, preservation of surface films, and increased work hardening.

The excerpt provides evidence that oxidation substantially mitigates galling in 316L stainless steel under self-mating contact, although it does not discuss 304 directly or establish a specific galling threshold stress for 304/316 contact. At low stress, the reported Rt values were approximately 780 μm for unoxidised material versus 26 μm for oxidised material; at higher stress, galled area was approximately 14% versus 1.2%, respectively. The excerpt describes the pressure-rise test for an evacuated vacuum vessel. Close the valve between the vessel and pump, measure the time Δt required for the pressure to increase by Δp, and repeat after repressurizing/pumping as appropriate. Once the pressure rise is attributed to a real leak rather than gas evolving from walls or seals, calculate the leak rate using qL = V × (Δp/Δt), where qL is in mbar·l/s (equivalent to mbar·L/s), V is the vessel volume in liters, and Δp/Δt is the pressure-rise rate in mbar/s. A real leak produces an approximately straight pressure-versus-time curve on linear axes; outgassing tends to taper toward a stable value, although both effects can coexist. The worked example uses V = 20 L, a pressure increase from 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻³ mbar over 300 s, yielding qL = 6×10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s.
